section_summary: This section (pages 513–587) of decimal file 894.00 covers Japanese internal political affairs and foreign relations from late November 1940 through January 1941, focusing heavily on the implementation of the 'New National Structure' and the Ten-Year Economic Plan for Greater East Asia. It details high-level cabinet reorganizations under Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoye, including the appointments of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma and Heisuke Yanagawa, alongside acute ministerial friction between Commerce Minister Ichizo Kobayashi and Vice Minister Nobusuke Kishi over state economic controls. Extensive despatches and telegrams from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and State Department memoranda analyze domestic dissatisfaction with the Tripartite Alliance, moderate maneuvering within the Japanese Navy, the diplomatic mission of Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura to Washington, and expanding Japanese pressures across China, French Indochina, and the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.about: Concludes a report examining whether the Imperial Rule Assistance Association threatens the constitutional deliberative role of the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Despatch assures IRAA won't usurp the Diet's constitutional role, with Konoye affirming constitutional adherence while testing whether totalitarian substance can coexist with parliamentary form.
subfiles.title: The Imperial Rule Assistance Association and Constitutional Parliamentary Government

subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy Tokyo's despatch transmitting candid anti-Axis and anti-expansionist remarks made by Japanese academics and a mining executive.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Coville summarizes Takagi, Kanda, and Uramatsu's alarm over the Tripartite Pact, with Uramatsu calling South Seas domination financially unsustainable given Korea's slow 30-year profitability.
subfiles.title: Tokyo's Despatch No. 5163: Comment of Certain Japanese Individuals on the Present Situation in Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Transmits critical assessments of Japan's foreign policy and the Tripartite Pact made by intellectual and business figures in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays Takagi calling the Tripartite Pact a grave U.S.-relations mistake, Kanda's pessimism over rising German influence and rumored Gestapo agents, and Uramatsu's view of southward conquest as economic folly.
subfiles.title: Comment of Certain Japanese Individuals on the Present Situation in Japan (Despatch No. 5163)

subfiles.about: Indexes a confidential telegram recording views on Japanese cabinet instability and responsibility for the Axis pact.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Telegram 1171 notes Chungking-Wang Ching-wei recognition talks and Paks predicting a Japanese government change, blaming the German pact on Konoye and Matsuoka.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Negotiations with Chungking Government for Recognition of Wang Ching-wei Government

subfiles.about: Summarizes American editorial commentary regarding Japanese recognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime, southward expansion, Admiral Nomura's appointment, and Prince Saionji's death.
subfiles.summary: Department relays American press calling Japan's Wang Ching-wei recognition an ominous joke, doubting Southeast Asian ambitions given China overextension, demanding good faith from Nomura, and mourning Saionji as liberalism's end.
subfiles.title: Editorial Comment in the American Press on Far Eastern Questions (Telegram No. 543)

subfiles.about: Reports late-night political activity indicating Premier Konoye's intention to reorganize and strengthen his cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports late-night talks suggesting Konoye may add a third Minister without Portfolio amid business discontent over the new economic structure.
subfiles.title: Speculation on Cabinet Reorganization to Strengthen Konoye Government (Telegram No. 1359)

subfiles.about: Confirms the official appointment of Baron Hiranuma as Home Minister and General Yanagawa as Justice Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports rumored cabinet changes with Yanagawa confirmed as Justice Minister and Hiranuma as Home Affairs Minister, other posts unannounced.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Reshuffle: Appointments of Hiranuma and Yanagawa (Telegram No. 1360)

subfiles.about: Transmits an extensive intelligence appraisal of naval moderation, German pressure, domestic economic discontent, and diplomatic hesitation.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew assesses intelligence indicating that the Japanese Navy is quietly exerting a moderate influence to avoid war with the United States and favors the eventual return of Admiral Yonai to the premiership. The Navy backed Admiral Nomura's appointment to Washington, conscious of army mechanization deficiencies and the need to complete capital ship construction, though it warns that joint Anglo-American use of Singapore would provoke military retaliation. Concurrently, Germany is seeking to drive Japan into war with the U.S. to curb aid to Britain, while Prince Konoye and other senior officials privately harbor deep regret over the Tripartite Alliance and Matsuoka's provocative diplomacy. The appointment of Baron Hiranuma as Home Minister is aimed at controlling domestic rightist discontent over the New Structure, while southward advances remain suspended pending negotiations with Moscow, Indochina, and the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.title: Assessment of Japanese Naval Moderation, Axis Ties, and Domestic Discontent (Telegram No. 1372)

subfiles.about: Provides a full Department paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's December 24 confidential telegram on Japanese naval and diplomatic posture.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This internal State Department paraphrase prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reproduces the substance of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 1372 for distribution to military and naval intelligence. It details the Japanese Navy's desire to avoid hostilities with the United States, its backing of Admiral Nomura, and its cautionary stance regarding Singapore. It notes German attempts to embroil Japan in war, mounting domestic dismay over the Axis pact and Foreign Minister Matsuoka, and Prime Minister Konoye's domestic rebalancing via Baron Hiranuma amid stalled northward and southward diplomatic maneuvers.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 1372 on Japanese Navy's Stance and Internal Politics

subfiles.about: Reports the imperial investiture of Takio Izawa to the Japanese Privy Council.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Izawa's Privy Council investiture, noting his past roles as Metropolitan Police chief, Taiwan Governor-General, and Tokyo mayor.
subfiles.title: Investiture of Takio Izawa as Privy Councilor (Telegram No. 1377)

subfiles.about: Reports a high-level rift in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry between Minister Kobayashi and Vice Minister Kishi over the New Economic Structure.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports open conflict between Commerce Minister Kobayashi and Vice Minister Kishi over the New Economic Structure, with Kobayashi demanding Kishi's refused resignation amid business resistance to planned economy.
subfiles.title: Conflict between Commerce Minister Kobayashi and Vice Minister Kishi over Economic Structure (Telegram No. 1384)

subfiles.about: Summarizes key findings of Embassy Tokyo's comprehensive monthly political and economic report for November 1940.
subfiles.from: Herbert P. Fales (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Fales reviews Despatch 5218 (November 1940): anxiety over U.S. Tripartite Pact reaction, Nomura's non-automatic-war statement, Hainan troop buildup, Batavia's refusal, alliance rumors, and denials the new structure is socialism.
subfiles.title: Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 5218: Report of Conditions in Japan During November 1940
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Transmits Embassy Tokyo's comprehensive monthly report detailing Japanese-American relations, foreign policy, imperial celebrations, and the Ten-Year Economic Plan for November 1940.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits Report No. 1670 surveying political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during November 1940. In U.S.-Japan relations, the report details diplomatic representations over Japanese attacks on American aviation and property in China, the detention of Vice Consul Rinden and Melville Jacoby in Hanoi, exchange restrictions, the formal appointment of Admiral Nomura, and Japanese reactions to President Roosevelt's reelection. In external relations, it covers the formal recognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime at Nanking, economic negotiations with French Indochina and the Netherlands East Indies, and border friction in Thailand. Internally, the report chronicles the 2,600th imperial anniversary celebrations, the death of Prince Saionji, the announcement of the Ten-Year Economic Plan for Greater East Asia, the creation of the South Seas Bureau, and growing debates over the New National Structure and state economic control.
subfiles.title: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of November 1940 (Despatch No. 5218, Report No. 1670)
